description: We are a multidisciplinary team from Bahrain’s Nasser Scientific and Technical Center (NCST), proudly participating in the NASA challenge. Passionate about space exploration, software development, AI, and data analysis, we aim to transform complex lunar mission challenges into innovative solutions. Through Lunar Landing Site Navigator, we strive to make Moon landing site analysis more accessible, intuitive, and efficient, contributing to the future of space exploration through teamwork, creativity, and determination.
summary: LUNARIS is a free web app that helps mission planners, educators and the public choose and compare landing sites at the Moon's south pole. For any site and hour it shows where the Sun and Earth are relative to the real terrain horizon, how much of the Sun is visible, how much solar energy is available, and when direct-to-Earth communication is geometrically possible (Earth above the skyline and a NASA Deep Space Network complex seeing the Moon). Users can compare up to four sites, or one site on four dates, side by side, with synchronized charts and a score whose arithmetic is shown. LUNARIS then goes one step further: it checks slope hazards across the whole landing ellipse and plans a sun-aware rover route that avoids moving shadows and protects the battery. Every number comes from NASA LRO LOLA terrain and the JPL DE421 ephemeris, computed by our own code and checked against JPL Horizons (max 0.003° for Sun/Earth, 0.0013° for DSN geometry) and a published LOLA illumination study (89.2% vs 88.1%). In a test of 300 departure times, sun-aware planning brought the rover back 42% more often than a shortest-path plan.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

LUNARIS ("Land, then drive") is an interactive lunar mission planning web app for the south pole. It answers the challenge question - which site and which date give the best solar power and direct-to-Earth communication - and then the next question a real mission faces: can we land safely, and can a rover reach a cold-trap target and come back before the moving shadows drain its battery?

PAGES

- South Pole Map: zoomable NASA LOLA shaded-relief map with six analysed regions (including the IM-2 Athena CLPS landing site). Zoom in to see our 40 m sunlight layer; click to compare or open a site.

- Sun & Earth: for any site and hour - Sun and Earth azimuth/elevation, the terrain skyline in that direction, visible fraction of the solar disc, Earth line of sight, which DSN complexes (Goldstone, Madrid, Canberra) see the Moon, a skyline panorama with Sun and Earth paths, sunlight and communication windows, and solar energy per day.

- Compare Sites: 2-4 sites from any region, or one site on up to 4 dates. Winner card with the worked score, side-by-side bars, exact numbers, three synchronized timeline charts and CSV export with provenance. Goals: Balanced, Power first, Earth contact first, or a custom weight.

- Landing Safety: slope hazard inside the whole landing ellipse, six weighted criteria with visible formulas, 90-day best-landing-date scan.

- Traverse Planner: shortest route vs sun-aware, time-dependent route with a battery model and departure-window finder.

- What If? Simulator: landing delays, longer shadows, Earth-link outage, blocked route, less solar power - before/after with reasons.

- Data & Sources: provenance of every layer, methods, validation and limits.

HOW IT WORKS

A Python pipeline computes terrain horizons for every 40 m cell in 72 directions (with lunar curvature and a 300 km far-field scan), then hourly sunlight, Earth line of sight, slope and permanently shadowed areas for all of 2027. Sun and Earth directions come from the JPL DE421 ephemeris with the IAU lunar rotation model. DSN geometry uses the same ephemeris at each complex. The React + TypeScript web app runs the scoring, comparison and a time-dependent A* rover planner over (cell, hour, battery) directly in the browser.

VALIDATION (all PASS)

- Sun and Earth directions vs NASA JPL Horizons: max difference 0.003 degrees over 8,761 hourly samples.

- Sunlight on real terrain vs Barker et al. (2021): 89.2% vs 88.1% published (Connecting Ridge, 5 m mast).

- Moon elevation at Goldstone vs JPL Horizons: max 0.0013 degrees; 721/721 hours agree on visibility.

- 57/57 planner checks, 52/52 Sun & Earth engine checks, 25/25 automated browser steps (including phone width).

KEY RESULT

Across 300 departure times in 5 regions, the sun-aware planner brought the rover back 193 times vs 136 for a shortest-path plan (+42%). Example: Malapert Massif, 15 Jan 2027 - the shortest path drops below the 20% battery reserve after 4.3 h; the sun-aware path finishes the 4.2 km trip with 32% left.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

One tool links site choice, landing safety and the first rover traverse, so planners, students and the public can see trade-offs quickly and check every number. Communication is shown honestly in three levels: line of sight (computed), a DSN complex sees the Moon (computed), and a real link (needs a scheduled antenna - not modelled).

TOOLS

Python (NumPy, SciPy, Skyfield), React, TypeScript, Vite, three.js, Recharts, Playwright for testing, GitHub Pages for hosting.

CREATIVITY AND FACTORS CONSIDERED

We studied existing tools first and focused on what they do not do: moving-shadow rover planning with a battery, ellipse-wide hazards, date-vs-date comparison and What-If. We considered data accuracy, transparency (formulas visible), honest limits (no boulders under ~40 m, ideal solar panel, no DSN scheduling), accessibility and phone layouts.

LINKS

Live app: https://saoudbumjaid.github.io/LUNARIS/

Code and documentation: https://github.com/SaoudBumjaid/LUNARIS

Independent student prototype by Team Karak & Cosmos (NCST, Kingdom of Bahrain). Not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.
dataRefs: NASA LRO LOLA south pole DEMs (Barker et al. 2023, NASA GSFC PGDA)
NASA PDS Geosciences Node - LRO LOLA polar elevation data (LDEM, 400 m far-field terrain)
NASA JPL Horizons System (validation of Sun, Earth and Moon directions)
NASA JPL Planetary and Lunar Ephemerides (DE421)
NASA Deep Space Network (station locations for communication geometry)
NASA GSFC PGDA - High-Resolution LOLA Topography for Lunar South Pole Sites (5 m, used for site locations)
NASA GSFC PGDA - Lunar Polar Illumination maps (used to place the Malapert Massif site)
projectRefs: Lunar Horizon / CLPS-MOON-BROWSER (MIT) - open 400 m LOLA terrain file used for far horizons
LUNAR//OPS (Apache-2.0) - open 20 m LOLA terrain patches for the six regions
Barker et al. (2021), Planetary and Space Science 203:105119 - published illumination used for validation
Skyfield (MIT) - astronomy library used with JPL DE421
Open-source web stack: React, Vite, three.js, Recharts (full list in package.json)
Claude by Anthropic - AI assistant used for coding, debugging, writing and slides (team reviewed all work)
